stem: Aarav starts at $7$ and applies the Collatz rule: if the current term is even, halve it; if it is odd, take $3n+1$. He writes $7$, $22$, $11$, $34$, $17$, $52$, $26$, $13$, $40$, $20$, $10$, $5$, $16$, $8$, $4$, $2$, $1$.

parts.text: Which claim correctly separates this chain from the Collatz conjecture?

options.text: The chain is one Collatz example that reaches $1$; it does not prove the rule for every whole-number start.
Reaching $1$ from $7$ proves that every whole-number start reaches $1$.
The Collatz rule applies only to even starts, so the odd terms such as $7$ and $11$ are mistakes.

parts.text: Give one reason for your choice.

part_answers.answer: One finished chain that reaches 1 is an example of the process; the conjecture claims every start reaches 1, which this single run cannot prove.

teacher.key_rationale: An example that reaches 1 is not a proof for every start. Treating one run as a universal proof, or banning odd starts, miss that distinction.
